properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31, delivering `req:export-says-what-it-cannot-carry` and closing the last open question under `cap:content-store`.

A COMMITTED MANIFEST, plain text, mapping CONTENT HASH → ORIGINAL FILENAME → WHAT REFERENCES IT. One artefact, two jobs, which is why it was chosen over either job's narrower answer:

1. COMPLETENESS. Once content exists, the export document holds only pointers, so handing someone `reflow2.json` alone gives them a design whose diagrams silently fail to resolve. The manifest makes "do I have everything?" a set comparison — hashes listed against hashes present — rather than a discovery made when a picture does not open. That is `req:content-reaches-every-seat`'s fail-loud requirement made checkable by a person, not only by the tool.

2. LEGIBILITY IN GIT. A content-addressed blob lands as `blobs/ab/cdef…` and git reports it as an added file with a hex name that tells a reviewer nothing. The manifest is text, so the same change also appears in a diff as a readable line — `architecture-sketch.png` added, referencing `dec:x` — which is what a human actually reads in `git log -p`.

`.gitattributes` MARKS THE BLOB DIRECTORY `binary`. Two concrete effects, and the second is the one that matters: git stops attempting diffs it cannot produce, and — critically — stops applying line-ending conversion, which would CORRUPT a PNG on a checkout configured for CRLF. That is silent data loss on someone else's machine, and one line prevents it.

WHY THE BINARY WORRY WAS SMALLER THAN IT LOOKED, recorded because the reasoning nearly went the other way. Git's weaknesses with binaries are poor diffs, poor delta compression, and unresolvable merge conflicts. IMMUTABLE CONTENT ADDRESSING removes two of the three outright: a blob is never updated, so an "edit" is a NEW FILE with a new name — git sees an addition, which is the clearest possible signal — and two people adding different blobs add different files, so a binary merge conflict cannot arise. The only conflict is on the pointer inside the export, which the `merge.reflow2` driver already handles. WHAT REMAINS IS GROWTH: every version is a new file that stays forever, and that is the size-cap question `dec:where-content-lives` deliberately left open.

DELIBERATELY NOT DECIDED HERE: whether the manifest lives inside the export document or beside it as its own committed file. Both satisfy the requirement; the second keeps the export byte-stable diff properties simpler and is the likelier answer, but it is an implementation choice for build time rather than a design commitment.
properties.name: A committed manifest — hash to filename to referenced-by — plus .gitattributes marking blobs binary
properties.rationale:
Taken because one artefact answered two questions that arrived independently — the export-completeness gap found by an impact-check, and Anthony's worry about git legibility for binaries. When a single small thing satisfies two unrelated needs, that is usually the right shape rather than a coincidence.

The `.gitattributes` line is the part with a real failure behind it rather than an inconvenience: line-ending conversion silently corrupting a binary on a differently-configured checkout is the kind of fault that appears as "the diagram is broken on my machine" weeks later, with nothing in the history to point at.

The binary-churn analysis is recorded because the initial framing — mine — overstated the problem, and correcting it is what made the manifest a legibility feature rather than a workaround. Content addressing had already solved most of what was being worried about; naming which part it did NOT solve (growth) is what keeps the remaining risk visible instead of assumed handled.
